name: Corniche & Ain Diab
hero_subtitle: Casablanca’s oceanfront promenade: beach clubs, cafés and Atlantic sunsets along seven kilometres of coast.

overview.title: The City’s Living Room by the Sea
overview.p1: The Corniche stretches along Ain Diab and is where Casablancans come to walk, meet friends and watch the ocean. Beach clubs, cafés and seafood restaurants line the route; the Hassan II Mosque sits at the northern end and anchors the skyline.
overview.p2: It is not a wild beach destination — the Atlantic here is often rough — but it is one of the best places in the city for a long walk, a coffee with a view, or a relaxed dinner facing the water.
overview.p3: Come at the end of the day when the light softens and the promenade fills with local families. Combine it easily with a visit to the mosque or a taxi hop to the restaurants further south.

food.title: Where to Eat on the Corniche
food.p1: The Corniche is lined with cafés, beach clubs and seafood restaurants. Pick a terrace with a view rather than the first invitation you get.
food.li1: Fresh fish and seafood at restaurants facing the ocean.
food.li2: Beach-club menus for a longer lunch or an evening drink.
food.li3: Simple cafés for coffee, juice and a short break from the wind.
food.li4: Ice cream and snacks for a casual stroll stop.
food.li5: Hotel and resort restaurants if you want a more formal table.
food.p2: Prices vary widely between a simple café and a full seafood restaurant. Check the menu before you sit down, especially on the more tourist-facing stretches.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting the Corniche & Ain Diab

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: Taxis and most walking routes end at the square, so it's an easy landmark to give a driver. Insist on the meter (compteur) in petit taxis. Cars can't enter the medina alleys, so your riad may ask you to meet a porter at the edge.

2.title: Photos and Performers
2.desc: Musicians, street offers artists and snake handlers expect a tip if you photograph them, so ask first and agree on an amount. Many travellers skip acts that use chained monkeys or snakes; you'll find plenty to watch without them.

3.title: Staying Comfortable
3.desc: It gets crowded and loud, so wear your bag in front and keep your phone out of back pockets. If someone grabs your hand to start a street offers design, just pull away politely and keep walking. Unofficial guides will offer to lead you somewhere; a firm no, thank you is enough.

q1.question: Is the Corniche free to visit?
q1.answer: Yes. The promenade is free and open to everyone. Beach clubs and restaurants set their own prices if you go inside.

q2.question: What is the best time to visit the Corniche?
q2.answer: Late afternoon through sunset is the most pleasant: cooler air, soft light and a lively local atmosphere. Morning is quieter for photos.

q3.question: Can you swim at Ain Diab?
q3.answer: The Atlantic can be rough and currents strong. Many visitors prefer the promenade and beach clubs over open-water swimming. Follow local advice and flagged areas.

q4.question: How long should I spend there?
q4.answer: Allow 1–2 hours for a walk and a coffee. Longer if you stay for dinner or combine it with the Hassan II Mosque at the northern end.

q5.question: How do I get to the Corniche from the city centre?
q5.answer: A short taxi ride (or ride-hail) from the centre or the mosque is the easiest option. The tram and buses also serve nearby stops; check current lines on the day.
